ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure is a circle, and A, B, C, D are all on the circle; A is at the lower left, B is at the upper left, C is above, and D is on the right side. Chord AC and chord BD intersect inside the circle at point E. In the figure, ∠AED is labeled as 95°, and arc AD is labeled as 120°. Reasoning: For an angle formed by two chords intersecting inside a circle, m∠AED = 1/2(arc AD + arc BC). Substitute 95 = 1/2(120 + arc BC), obtaining 190 = 120 + arc BC, so arc BC = 70°. ∠BAC is an inscribed angle intercepting arc BC, therefore m∠BAC = 1/2 × 70 = 35°.

raw_record.question_text: If $m \angle AED = 95$ and $m \widehat{AD} = 120$, what is $m \angle BAC$?

method.method_draft: Read the diagram as a circle with chords AC and BD intersecting at E; A, B, C, D lie on the circle in that cyclic order, and ∠AED is the interior angle formed by the two intersecting chords. From the text, use m∠AED = 95 and m arc AD = 120. Apply the intersecting-chords angle theorem: m∠AED = 1/2(m arc AD + m arc BC). Solve 95 = 1/2(120 + arc BC), giving arc BC = 70. Since ∠BAC is an inscribed angle intercepting arc BC, m∠BAC = 1/2·70 = 35.

method.method_draft: Read the diagram as two chords AC and BD crossing at E, with D, E, B collinear and A, E, C collinear. From the text, m∠AED = 95 and m arc AD = 120. Instead of using ∠AED directly for arc BC, take the adjacent angle ∠AEB, which is supplementary to ∠AED, so m∠AEB = 180 − 95 = 85. By the intersecting-chords theorem, m∠AEB = 1/2(m arc AB + m arc CD), so arc AB + arc CD = 170. The full circle is arc AB + arc BC + arc CD + arc AD = 360; with arc AD = 120, get arc BC = 360 − 120 − 170 = 70. Finally, ∠BAC is an inscribed angle intercepting arc BC, so m∠BAC = 35.
